FREA: A Multi-Source Expert Benchmark for
Reaction Feasibility Verification

Botao Yu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State University    Bo Zhou Affiliation: Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Illinois Chicago    Daniel Adu-Ampratwum Affiliation: College of Pharmacy, The Ohio State University    Frazier N. Baker Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State University Affiliation: Department of Biomedical Informatics, The Ohio State University    Ziru Chen Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State University    Reza Averly Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State University    Ye Liu Affiliation: Department of Biomedical Informatics, The Ohio State University    Wenhao Gao Affiliation: Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, University of Pennsylvania    Xia Ning Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State University Affiliation: College of Pharmacy, The Ohio State University Affiliation: Department of Biomedical Informatics, The Ohio State University Affiliation: Translational Data Analytics Institute, The Ohio State University    Huan Sun Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Ohio State University
Abstract

As generative models and AI agents propose chemical reactions at a scale beyond expert review, feasibility verifiers decide which proposals enter synthesis planning. But do their decisions agree with chemists across different kinds of candidates? We introduce FREA, a benchmark of 751751 reactions labeled by expert chemists under an explicit feasibility criterion, drawn from retrosynthesis model proposals, zero-yield experimental records, edits by large language models (LLMs), and five negative candidate generation methods. Our evaluation finds that no verifier leads across all sources: LLMs given only the criterion are competitive with dedicated verifiers, while forward models perform best on retrosynthesis proposals but reject most feasible edits of recorded reactions at the evaluated operating points. Looking beyond aggregate scores, both forward models perform below chance when separating infeasible alternative disconnections from feasible generated candidates. To study whether negative supervision addresses these weaknesses, we also release a corpus of over 14 million recorded reactions and generated negative candidates. In matched training comparisons, adding a mixture of generated negatives to forward training raises mean AUROC across sources, but these gains do not extend to retrosynthesis proposals. Varying the generation method further shows that the largest gain on generated candidates coincides with worse proposal screening. These findings motivate evaluating verifiers against experts across sources and designing negatives for transfer to model proposals. The benchmark and corpus are publicly available.

1 Introduction

Generative models, search-based planning systems and language-model agents now propose chemical reactions at a scale that no chemist can review one by one (Segler et al., 2018; Long et al., 2025; Baker et al., 2026). Within these pipelines, reaction feasibility verifiers act as gatekeepers that decide which proposals survive into downstream planning (Segler et al., 2018; Genheden et al., 2020a; Sadowski et al., 2025). Accepting an infeasible reaction can derail a plan, while rejecting a feasible alternative can eliminate a useful route. Reliable verification therefore becomes increasingly important as human review is removed from the loop.

Common verifiers include forward models, which use target-product recovery or likelihood as a proxy for feasibility (Schwaller et al., 2019b; Schwaller et al., 2020), and classifiers trained to separate recorded reactions from generated negatives (Segler et al., 2018; Genheden et al., 2020a; Gaiński et al., 2025), which are typically assessed by their effect on downstream search or on held-out generated reactions (Appendix A). Here, we ask: do verifiers that appear reliable on recorded or generated reactions agree with chemists on the reactions they are actually asked to screen?

Answering this question requires labels that are independent of how verifiers are built. Published reaction data favor successful outcomes (Voinarovska et al., 2024), while automatically generated negative candidates need not be infeasible. Expert-labeled reactions therefore provide a direct basis for evaluating feasibility verifiers.

We introduce FREA, an expert-labeled benchmark of 751751 reactions. A reaction is feasible if it lists all substantive reactants and admits reasonable conditions that yield the target products in isolable form (Section 3). The reactions come from four sources: proposals of eight retrosynthesis models, zero-yield experimental records, edits of recorded reactions by large language models (LLMs), and candidates from five negative candidate generation methods (Section 4). Annotators label each reaction without seeing its source.

Comparing LLMs, forward models and verifiers trained on generated negatives, we find that no verifier leads across all sources (Section 6.1). LLMs given only the criterion are competitive with dedicated verifiers, with Claude Opus 5 achieving the highest mean balanced accuracy. Forward models are strongest on retrosynthesis proposals, yet at the evaluated operating points they reject most feasible edits of recorded reactions.

Looking within the generated source reveals a sharper failure: the strongest verifiers of model proposals can rank infeasible candidates above feasible ones. Both forward models score below chance on alternative product disconnections, with AUROCs of 26.2 and 32.5 against the same feasible reference reactions (Section 6.2). Adding generated negatives to forward training improves this comparison and gives the highest mean AUROC across sources, but reduces performance on other constructions. These selective gains leave open whether negative supervision improves verification beyond particular constructions, especially on model proposals.

To test this, we use an accompanying corpus of over 14 million recorded reactions and generated negative candidates, with no benchmark reaction in the training data (Section C.5). In matched comparisons with continued forward training, the mean AUROC gain from a mixture of generated negatives does not extend to retrosynthesis proposals (Section 7). Varying the generation method further shows that the largest gain on generated candidates coincides with a decline on model proposals. The open challenge is therefore to generate negatives whose benefits extend to the proposals verifiers must screen.

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    An expert benchmark of 341341 feasible and 410410 infeasible reactions from four sources, labeled under an explicit criterion and released with recorded failure reasons (Sections 3 and 4).

  2. 2.

    An evaluation of verifier strengths and failure modes, across reaction sources and candidate generation methods (Sections 5 and 6).

  3. 3.

    A generated corpus and a controlled transfer study, with matched and pre-registered training comparisons that test whether negative supervision improves screening of model proposals and motivate hypotheses for negative-data design (Section 7).

2 Related Work

Feasibility filters.

Classifiers trained on recorded reactions and constructed negatives have been used in synthesis planning since the in-scope filter of Segler et al. (2018). AiZynthFinder uses template-generated negatives (Genheden et al., 2020b; Genheden et al., 2020a). RetroGFN combines forward-template negatives with replacements of the recorded product (Gaiński et al., 2025). RetroTrim combines several scorers and evaluates both individual reactions and complete routes by expert review (Sadowski et al., 2025). These studies establish the value of filtering in planning, but evaluation on generated negatives does not test whether the assigned negative labels agree with experts. FREA evaluates individual reactions across four sources under a common expert criterion.

Expert and precedent-based evaluation.

ChemCensor scores reactions by checking their reaction centers and functional-group context against recorded reactions (Zagribelnyy et al., 2026b). Concurrent work also evaluates retrosynthesis predictions against expert judgments (Zagribelnyy et al., 2026a). FREA combines model proposals with experimental records and multiple forms of controlled perturbation under an explicit feasibility criterion. This broader coverage supports both diagnosis of source-dependent failures and evaluation of transfer from generated negative training data.

Negative reaction data.

Published failures are scarce (Voinarovska et al., 2024). Existing resources include private laboratory records (Jiang et al., 2021), high-throughput experiments for acid–amine couplings (Zhong et al., 2025), and data for enzymatic reactions (Chainani et al., 2025). Experimental failures describe particular conditions. FREA uses zero-yield records as candidates for expert annotation and combines them with model proposals and constructed reactions. Appendix A gives a detailed comparison of these resources and adjacent approaches.

3 Reaction Feasibility Task Definition

Given reactants 𝐑={r1,…,rk}\mathbf{R}=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}\} and products 𝐏={p1,…,pm}\mathbf{P}=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{m}\}, a verifier predicts

f⁡(𝐑,𝐏)∈{0,1},f(\mathbf{R},\mathbf{P})\in\{0,1\}, (1)

where 1 denotes a feasible reaction and 0 an infeasible one. The input contains no reaction conditions, and 𝐏\mathbf{P} need not include every product of the reaction.

We define feasibility from the perspective of synthesis planning, in which a verifier screens retrosynthesis proposals. Each reaction is treated as a proposal, which is feasible if a planning system could keep it as a valid step of a route. Specifically, a feasible proposal must satisfy two conditions.

Completeness.

Completeness asks whether the proposal lists everything the step needs, apart from routine components. The proposal must list every substantive reactant required to produce the target products, rather than only a transformation from a main reactant to a product. Auxiliary components, which act in routine supporting roles such as catalysts, solvents, bases, reducing agents and water, may be assumed. Any species outside these roles is substantive. For example, a Suzuki coupling is incomplete without its organoboron partner and an esterification without its alcohol, whereas the water of a hydrolysis may be left implicit.

Reactivity.

Reactivity asks whether the listed reactants can actually give the target products. There must be reasonable conditions, compatible with the listed reactants and products, under which the listed reactants and any assumed auxiliary components give the target products in isolable form. The target products need not be the major products. The reaction must take place in a single step or a one-pot operation, without isolating an intermediate.

Rationale.

Both conditions follow from how proposals are produced and used in synthesis planning. A step in a route must be executable from its listed starting materials, so a proposal that omits a substantive partner cannot be kept. Retrosynthesis models, like the reaction databases they are trained on, often omit routine components (Schneider et al., 2016; Wigh et al., 2024), which a chemist supplies without comment. Requiring them would reject well-formed proposals, so auxiliary components may be assumed. Proposals also leave the conditions to the chemist, so reactivity depends on whether reasonable conditions exist, not on whether any are stated. A route only needs to isolate the products of a step and carry them forward, while the share of competing products depends on conditions that the proposal does not fix, so the target products need not be the major ones. A sequence that isolates an intermediate is two steps of a route, so a single step or a one-pot operation is required. Finally, the assumptions are limited to what a chemist routinely supplies. If any missing reactant, or any conditions however extreme, could be assumed, almost any product would be reachable from almost any reactants, and an infeasible label would carry no information.

What the labels assert.

The labels record expert judgments under this criterion, which follows how a chemist reviews a proposed step. They do not predict yield or certify experimental success. A zero-yield record can therefore be labeled feasible if other reasonable conditions could produce the target. Appendix B lists the permitted auxiliary roles and gives the full decision procedure and annotation protocol.

4 The FREA Benchmark

FREA provides a common test of whether verifiers agree with experts across different sources of reaction candidates. It contains 751751 expert-labeled reactions, with 341341 feasible and 410410 infeasible under Section 3. The four sources connect practical screening, targeted diagnosis, and evaluation of transfer (Table 1). Combining reactions encountered in practice with deliberate perturbations allows us to test whether a verifier’s strengths extend beyond one source.

4.1 Four Reaction Sources

Retrosynthesis proposals (RP).

We collect proposals from eight single-step retrosynthesis models for targets in ORDerly (Wigh et al., 2024), a curated dataset derived from the Open Reaction Database (Kearnes et al., 2021). The models span template-based (Chen & Jung, 2021), semi-template (Chen et al., 2023), and template-free approaches (Zeng et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024; Irwin et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2024; Baker et al., 2026). Proposals are retained whether or not they reproduce the recorded reactants. RP therefore tests the proposals that verifiers must screen during planning, including valid alternatives to the recorded reaction.

Zero-yield records (ZR).

These are ORDerly reactions with a reported yield of zero. They were attempted experimentally, but failure under the recorded conditions does not determine feasibility under our criterion. On the contrary, chemists presumably attempted them because they expected them to work. We therefore include them as potentially feasible reactions and leave their labels unsettled until expert annotation.

LLM perturbations (LP).

GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026a) and Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026a) are instructed to edit recorded reactions to make them infeasible while keeping them superficially coherent. This source challenges verifiers on identifying infeasible edits among superficially coherent reactions.

Generated reactions (GR).

We propose five methods for constructing negative candidates, building on earlier uses of template application and reaction component replacement (Segler et al., 2018; Genheden et al., 2020a; Gaiński et al., 2025). The methods differ in what they change (Figure 1):

  • •

    Random Addition (RA) adds atoms at reactant reaction centers.

  • •

    Random Replacement (RR) replaces the reactant set with a similar set from another recorded reaction.

  • •

    New Center (NC) chooses a different product disconnection and completes the resulting fragments into reactants (Chen et al., 2023; Baker et al., 2024).

  • •

    Forward Template (FT) applies an alternative forward template to the recorded reactants.

  • •

    Elementary Template (ET) applies a sequence of elementary reaction templates (Joung et al., 2024) to obtain a different product.

RA, RR and NC change the reactants while keeping the product. FT and ET change the product while keeping the reactants. We sample the same number of candidates from each method for annotation, retaining both feasible and infeasible examples. The known generation methods allow failures to be traced to specific constructions. Comparing GR with the other sources then tests whether gains on these constructions extend to other reactions. Applying the same methods to the curated ORDerly reactions also produces the generated corpus used for training in Section 7. Appendices C and D give data collection and generation details.

4.2 Expert Annotation

Two chemists, a pharmacy faculty member and a chemistry postdoctoral researcher with wet-laboratory experience, labeled reactions without seeing their sources or model predictions. The workflow combined guideline calibration, independent annotation and joint review of disagreements, yielding 751751 expert-labeled benchmark reactions. The release includes recorded failure reasons and notes where available. Appendix B gives the calibration procedure, inter-annotator agreement and adjudication details.

The expert labels illustrate why source alone cannot determine feasibility: 79 of 93 zero-yield records are judged feasible, as are 33 of 289 generated candidates intended to be negative. Expert labels therefore provide a reference that neither recorded outcomes nor generation procedures supply alone.

5 Evaluation Protocol

Evaluated systems.

We compare three groups of systems in the main results:

  • •

    LLMs. Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026b) and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b) receive the reactants, products and feasibility criterion, and return a decision with an explanation.

  • •

    Forward models. Chemformer (Irwin et al., 2022) and BARTSmiles (Chilingaryan et al., 2024) are fine-tuned on recorded reactions. Top-10 inclusion accepts a proposal if its target matches one of the ten highest-ranked product predictions after canonicalization. Log-likelihood (LL) scores the supplied target by its mean per-token log-probability given the reactants.

  • •

    Models trained on generated negatives. BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) continues the BARTSmiles forward model with a loss that favors recorded reactions over generated negative candidates, and is scored by LL. BARTSmiles (disc.) is trained to output a feasibility score directly. Descriptor GBDT is a gradient-boosted tree using 58 chemical descriptors. All three use the training split of the generated corpus, with no benchmark reaction in their training data (Section C.5).

We also evaluate a rule-based baseline and the released filter from the AiZynthFinder planning tool (Genheden et al., 2020b), with results in .

Metrics.

The primary metric is AUROC. We also report balanced accuracy (BAcc), the mean of the acceptance rate for feasible reactions and the rejection rate for infeasible reactions. BAcc covers all systems, including the LLM and top-10 decisions for which we extract no continuous score. Continuous-score thresholds are fixed on held-out generated pairs before application to FREA. We report results for each source and their unweighted mean across the four sources.

and  provide implementation details and the full evaluation protocol, including inference and training settings, model and threshold selection, and statistical tests.

6 Results

6.1 Performance Across Sources

We first ask whether verifiers agree with experts on each source, which determines how reliably they can act as gatekeepers. Table 2 reports AUROC and BAcc within each source, together with their unweighted means.

Frontier LLMs, given only the criterion, are strong candidate verifiers. Without examples from FREA or parameter updates, Claude Opus 5 achieves the highest four-source mean BAcc (68.0) and GPT-6 Astra reaches 65.7. They also lead on the two edited sources: Claude on LP (76.1 BAcc) and GPT on GR (62.7). Criterion prompting thus yields performance competitive with dedicated verifiers, together with textual rationales for expert inspection. However, they reject only 44.7–57.6% of infeasible RP proposals, and each rejects only 4 of the 14 infeasible ZR records (), leaving substantial false acceptance on these sources. In addition, the binary outputs used here do not support threshold tuning, while average API costs of US$0.040–0.059 per reaction limit their practicality at scale ().

Forward models are the strongest verifiers of retrosynthesis proposals, but reject most feasible edits of recorded reactions. BARTSmiles achieves the highest RP AUROC with likelihood scoring (78.9) and BAcc with top-10 inclusion (73.1). Yet at the evaluated operating points, the four forward-model readouts accept only 28.1–37.5% of feasible LP reactions and 12.1–33.3% of feasible GR reactions, compared with 94.9–98.7% on ZR (). A possible explanation is that forward models are trained to reproduce recorded reactions, so they may penalize LP and GR departures from recorded reaction patterns even when the edits preserve feasibility. Among the two readouts, we recommend LL in practice: it offers comparable BAcc within each backbone, avoids the cost of beam search, and supports threshold adjustment.

Generated negatives give the highest mean AUROC when added to a forward model’s training, whereas classifiers trained on them directly have the lowest. In Table 2, BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) achieves 75.2 mean AUROC, while BARTSmiles (disc.) and Descriptor GBDT have lower means than the original forward models. This contrast suggests that, in this comparison, generated negatives are more useful for supplementing forward prediction than for training a feasibility classifier directly. However, the gains of BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) come mainly from LP and GR and do not extend to RP, so its mean lead does not imply better screening of retrosynthesis proposals. We further study the effects of negative supervision in Section 7.

Overall, no verifier leads across all sources, indicating that agreement with experts varies by candidate source. For screening retrosynthesis proposals, BARTSmiles LL is a practical default among the evaluated systems, while LLMs can provide rationales for selective expert review. Use FREA as an initial benchmark, then validate the model and calibrate any score threshold on separate data representative of the intended application.

6.2 Performance by Generation Method

The differences across sources in Section 6.1 leave open whether performance is consistent across the constructions within a source. We examine this on GR, where each candidate’s generation method is known. Table 3 compares each method’s infeasible candidates with the same 33 feasible GR reactions drawn from all five methods.

Both forward models score below chance on NC negatives, ranking infeasible candidates above feasible reference reactions. NC generates alternative product disconnections. Chemformer achieves 26.2 AUROC (95% CI [15,37][15,37]) and BARTSmiles achieves 32.5 ([20,45][20,45]). Both intervals lie entirely below 50, indicating an inversion of the desired ranking on this comparison. The same models achieve 83.5–94.9 AUROC on FT and ET, which change the recorded product, and 79.8–83.5 on RR, which replaces the reactant set. Both are near chance on RA, which makes local reactant edits. Evaluation on FT, ET or RR alone would miss this failure on alternative disconnections.

BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) improves NC and RA scores but reduces RR performance relative to BARTSmiles LL. NC increases from 32.5 to 94.2 and RA from 46.1 to 72.7, while RR decreases from 79.8 to 53.4. The higher overall GR AUROC thus combines substantial gains and losses across methods. The discriminative verifier exhibits a similar profile and scores below BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) on four of the five methods.

To include systems that return only decisions, we also examine rejection rates (). Claude rejects at least 83% of infeasible candidates from each method, but also rejects two-thirds of the feasible GR reactions. Its high negative rejection rates must therefore be considered together with its rejection of feasible alternatives.

These comparisons show that source-level scores can conceal systematic failures on particular constructions. A separate analysis in shows that reaction-level performance also need not preserve expert rankings of retrosynthesis models.

For reaction-level verification, the selective gains of BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) leave a training question open: can generated negatives improve agreement with experts beyond specific constructions, especially on RP? We address this with matched training comparisons in Section 7.

7 Training with Generated Negatives

The preceding analyses locate failures tied to candidate construction. We now ask whether generated negatives can improve verification across sources, particularly on RP. Using generated training pairs that share no reaction with the benchmark (Section C.5), we first isolate the effect of adding negative supervision (Section 7.1), then vary its generation method (Section 7.2). Each setting uses a single training run, so the observed gains remain exploratory.

7.1 Adding Negative Supervision

The comparison in Section 6.1 does not isolate negative supervision from continued forward training. To separate their effects, we compare BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) with a control that starts from the same BARTSmiles forward model and uses the same positive reactions and training schedule. Both runs continue for one epoch over 800,000800,000 pairs (). The control optimizes only the forward-prediction loss. BARTSmiles (LL ++ neg.) adds a preference loss that ranks each recorded reaction above its generated candidate, using the same mean per-token log-likelihood as at evaluation. This preserves forward-prediction training while introducing supervision from the negative candidates.

The observed mean gain is concentrated outside retrosynthesis proposals. The four-source mean AUROC increases from 71.4 for the continued-training control to 75.2 with negatives (Table 4). The starting model scores 72.8, so the gain is not reproduced by the additional epoch of positive-only training. Scores increase on ZR, LP and GR, but decrease slightly on RP.

Repeating the comparison with 2,400,0002,400,000 pairs gives the same directions of change (). None of the within-source differences survives Holm correction (). Because these runs use a mixture of generated negatives, they leave open whether the lack of RP improvement is shared across generation methods or depends on the mixture.

7.2 Choosing the Generation Method

To examine this possibility, we vary the generation method supplying the training pairs. This complements Section 6.2, which varied test constructions for fixed verifiers: here we measure how training on different negatives transfers across sources. We compare each method alone, an equal mixture of all five, and a control without negatives. All seven runs share the initialization, positive stream for forward prediction and training schedule. Each run with negatives uses 800,000800,000 pairs; only the pairs supplied to the preference loss change. We evaluate all runs at their final training step under the pre-registered design ().

The observed rankings of generation methods differ between GR and RP. In these runs, NC raises GR AUROC by 12.1 points but lowers RP by 2.8 points (Table 5). RR raises mean AUROC by 3.2 points, followed by the mixture at 2.3 points, while ET leaves the mean nearly unchanged. Both RR and RA slightly improve RP over the control. The equal mixture has a lower mean than RR and also lowers RP by 2.3 points.

Only the FT decline of 6.4 points in mean AUROC is significant after Holm correction (padj=0.001p_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.001). The RR gain has padj=0.08p_{\mathrm{adj}}=0.08, leaving its benefit over the control inconclusive. FT also has the lowest estimated negative purity—the fraction of candidates experts judge infeasible—at 77.2%, compared with about 93% for RR, NC and ET (Table C.1). FT’s decline therefore cannot be attributed to its construction independently of label noise. Together with the differing outcomes of RR, NC and ET, this motivates examining label reliability alongside other properties of the generated candidates.

7.3 Hypotheses for Improving Generalization

The method comparison shows that gains on generated constructions need not carry over to RP, but leaves the reasons for this limited transfer open. We therefore combine the training results with expert label audits and the descriptor-classifier analysis to formulate three hypotheses for improving negative-data design. Each requires a separate test.

Validating negative labels may improve transfer by preserving feasible alternatives. FT combines the lowest estimated negative purity with the largest performance decline. Since generated candidates can remain feasible, assigning them negative labels can penalize valid alternatives to the recorded reaction. This motivates expert audits of recurring labeling errors, followed by comparisons that filter or down-weight uncertain candidates while holding the generation method fixed.

Reducing simple descriptor differences may encourage more transferable learning. Label reliability alone may not account for the outcomes: RR, NC and ET have comparable estimated purities but different observed transfer patterns. Among these three, RR candidates are the hardest for the descriptor classifier to separate from recorded reactions (), and RR gives the largest observed mean gain. This association motivates testing generation methods that match recorded reactions and negative candidates on simple molecular descriptors while controlling label purity.

Targeting errors in model proposals may improve transfer more than simply mixing generation methods. Beyond label reliability and descriptor differences, useful negatives should address the errors encountered in model proposals. The NC and mixture runs both improve GR while lowering RP, motivating a test of candidates targeted to those errors. Expert-reviewed proposals from a separate development set could identify recurring errors and guide perturbations and method weights. Held-out proposals would then test whether these targeted choices improve transfer.

8 Conclusion

FREA provides an expert reference for reaction feasibility verification across multiple candidate sources. Its results reveal complementary strengths: criterion-prompted LLMs are competitive with dedicated verifiers, while forward models lead on retrosynthesis proposals yet fail systematically on some constructed candidates. No verifier leads across all sources, and strong aggregate performance can conceal these failures. Verifiers should therefore be selected and calibrated on data representative of their intended screening task.

Our matched training experiments show how the benchmark can guide improvement: adding a mixture of generated negatives raises mean AUROC without improving performance on model proposals, while transfer varies with the generation method. This makes performance on those proposals a central test for negative-data design. The results motivate testing whether auditing negative labels, controlling descriptor differences and targeting recurring proposal errors improve transfer. These directions remain hypotheses given the benchmark’s limited coverage, judgment uncertainty and single-run training comparisons (). Together, the benchmark and accompanying corpus support developing verifiers whose improvements are measured against expert judgments on the reactions they must screen.

Appendix A Related Work, Extended

This appendix expands Section 2 and compares the resources it mentions (Table A.1).

Filters trained on constructed negatives.

Segler et al. (2018) introduced an in-scope filter: a neural classifier trained to distinguish recorded reactions from constructed ones. Its 100100 million training negatives were generated by forward rule application and negative sampling; Genheden et al. (2020a), who reimplemented the filter, describe the two strategies as taking the further products that the recorded template yields on the recorded reactants (3030 million) and applying a randomly chosen template to a random reactant set (7070 million). AiZynthFinder ships a filter built on the same principle, and Genheden et al. (2020a) compare three ways of drawing the negatives, all template-based and all keeping the recorded reactants: applying the recorded template to give a further product, applying a random template, and applying a template suggested by a recommender. RetroGFN’s reaction feasibility model is trained on negatives from two procedures, applying forward templates to the recorded reactants to obtain a product that was not recorded, and swapping the recorded product for another product of high Tanimoto similarity (Gaiński et al., 2025). The same paper separately builds a set of hard negatives in the way our RR method does, pairing a template-generated product with reactant sets of high Tanimoto similarity to the ones it was generated from, and uses that set to estimate how often a forward model accepts an infeasible reaction, which is the measurement Section 6 makes against expert labels instead. RetroTrim assembles an ensemble of scorers, some learned and some derived from reaction databases, and shows that different scorers catch different classes of hallucinated reaction. It evaluates reaction scores against expert labels and complete routes for 32 targets (Sadowski et al., 2025). Its reaction-level evaluation treats Safe Bet as positive and Rather Not and Nonsense as negative, excluding Worthwhile reactions. Filters in this line of work have been assessed on constructed test reactions and through their effects on downstream search; Genheden et al. (2020a) also test transfer between negative generation methods.

Evaluation based on precedent.

Zagribelnyy et al. (2026b) argue that scoring single-step retrosynthesis by exact match against one recorded answer penalizes valid alternatives, and propose instead to extract a proposed reaction’s reaction center and its surrounding functional-group context and check both against a relational database of reported reactions, assigning a score of zero when no precedent is found. They release CREED, a corpus of 22,712,52622,712,526 reactions for 1,493,7151,493,715 products generated from roughly 3,000 expert-written bidirectional templates. Precedent-based scoring is complementary to our expert judgments, which can accept a sound proposal without a matching recorded precedent. CREED supplies plausible generated reactions for training. FREA combines feasible and infeasible expert-labeled candidates across four sources to evaluate verifiers and the transfer of generated-negative training.

Negative reactions from experiment.

Jiang et al. (2021) trained on failed reactions recorded in a private industrial laboratory notebook, a resource that is not public. Zhong et al. (2025) released high-throughput experimentation data for acid–amine couplings with Bayesian deep learning, including observed failures under specified conditions for a single reaction class. DORA-XGB builds an enzymatic reaction feasibility classifier, taking unreported reactions as infeasible (Chainani et al., 2025); the assumption is strong and the domain is retrobiosynthesis. Zero-yield records are plentiful in public databases (Kearnes et al., 2021; Wigh et al., 2024) but report an outcome under particular conditions, so they cannot by themselves establish that a transformation is impossible. This is why our ZR source enters the benchmark as candidates for annotation rather than as negatives.

Feasibility from first principles.

Rappoport & Aspuru-Guzik (2019) explore reaction pathways with heuristically aided quantum chemistry, and Sigmund et al. (2025) combine quantum-chemical descriptors with machine learning to predict feasibility and selectivity for one reaction type. Mechanistic datasets support models that reproduce elementary steps (Joung et al., 2024). Mechanistic and energetic evidence from these approaches could complement expert review of difficult proposals in future extensions.

Adjacent tasks.

Yield prediction asks how much product forms under stated conditions rather than whether a proposal is well formed, and its own difficulties are documented (Voinarovska et al., 2024). Forward reaction prediction asks what products form (Schwaller et al., 2019a; Irwin et al., 2022; Chilingaryan et al., 2024), and is repurposed for verification by the round-trip convention (Schwaller et al., 2019b; Maziarz et al., 2025) that Section 6 evaluates.

Appendix B Feasibility Criterion and Annotation Protocol

This appendix states the criterion of Section 3 in full and gives its rationale (Sections B.1 and B.2), specifies what annotators record (Sections B.3, B.4 and B.5), and describes how the evaluation set was annotated (Sections B.6, B.7, B.8 and B.9).

B.1 Criterion

For each reaction, the annotator decides whether, under some reasonable conditions, the listed reactants can give the listed products in isolable form, in a single step or a credible one-pot operation. Only the reactant and product lists are given; there are no separate fields for reagents, conditions or yield. Any species explicitly listed on the reactant side remains part of the proposal. The judgment combines the two conditions of Section 3, which are applied as follows.

Completeness.

Every species on the left-hand side counts as a reactant, whether or not a reaction database would record it as a reagent; what matters is whether an omitted species is essential. An omitted species may be assumed only if it acts in one of the permitted roles of Table B.1, within the scope stated there. Such a species is auxiliary. Anything else is substantive and may not be assumed. A transformation evidently intended as a Suzuki coupling is not a complete proposal without its organoboron partner, and an esterification written without its alcohol is not one either. Status follows from the role a species plays here, not from its name, size or customary classification (Table B.2), so methanol is auxiliary as a solvent and substantive as the source of a methyl ester. A missing substantive reactant makes a reaction infeasible even when the intended transformation is recognizable.

A proposal that is complete but for a permitted auxiliary carries a missing_auxiliary_reagent note naming the species and its role (Section B.5).

The test is structural, not stoichiometric.

The test cannot be implemented by comparing element counts, which fail in both directions. Counts can balance although a substantive partner is missing, because leaving groups and other listed species routinely supply the same elements. In one proposal from our pool, a substrate and the coupling reagent HATU are offered as giving a product that bears a 2-picolylamine group; the element counts balance, since HATU supplies carbon, nitrogen and oxygen, yet no listed species contains a picolylamine fragment, so the amine partner is missing. Conversely, counts can fail to balance although nothing is missing: the test concerns only atoms retained in the products, so omitted by-products, unspecified stoichiometry and differences in hydrogen count are not defects, provided a credible hydrogen source exists among the permitted additions. Annotators are therefore asked where each fragment of the products comes from, structurally, rather than whether the formula balances.

Reactivity.

The annotator may assume any reasonable conditions that are not stated, including solvent, temperature, time, atmosphere and order of addition, but may not replace, modify or disregard a listed species. A reaction satisfies reactivity if, under some such conditions, the listed reactants, completed only by auxiliary species, give the listed products in a form that can be isolated. They may form alongside other products, which need not be listed. What is required is that the listed products can be obtained and separated. Assumed conditions must remain compatible with the reactants and products; hypothetical extreme conditions cannot rescue an otherwise unsupported transformation. The reaction must take place in a single step or a credible one-pot operation, which may include sequential addition and the in situ formation of a reactive species; workup does not count as a separate step, whereas the isolation of an intermediate does. A reaction fails this condition only if no reasonable conditions would yield the listed products.

B.2 Rationale and scope

Why an explicit definition is needed.

Feasibility is used in the synthesis-planning literature in at least four senses: a reaction may be called feasible because it is recorded in a database, recoverable by a forward model from its reactants, precedented in its reaction center and functional-group context, or executable in a laboratory. These senses agree on routine transformations but diverge on the cases that matter most for evaluation: an unprecedented but sound disconnection may be executable, whereas a precedented transformation applied to an incompatible substrate is not. A benchmark must therefore state which sense it measures. Ours is the validity of a retrosynthesis proposal, judged by experts under the rules of this appendix.

Why the two conditions are defined this way.

The criterion reflects chemical practice and the requirements of synthesis planning. Chemical practice. A chemist reviewing a proposed step reads everything on the left-hand side as reactants and judges an omission by whether the omitted species is essential: a solvent, water or a routine additive is supplied without comment, a partner that builds part of the product is not. Because a proposal specifies no conditions, the chemist likewise asks whether reasonable conditions exist, not whether particular conditions are stated. Application. In retrosynthesis planning, a proposal that omits a routine component still describes a usable step and should be expanded, whereas one that omits the coupling partner does not describe a step at all and should be pruned. A step is useful in a route if its product can be isolated and carried forward, and how the material divides among competing products depends on conditions that a proposal does not fix, so reactivity asks only that the listed products can be isolated. Informativeness. If any unlisted species could be assumed, or any conditions however extreme, almost any product would be reachable from almost any reactants, and a negative label would carry no information.

What the label asserts.

A positive label requires more than a recognizable transformation, as the completeness condition makes explicit. A negative label denotes a defect in the proposal as stated; it does not assert that the transformation is impossible under every conceivable condition, a claim that expert annotation cannot establish. Proposal feasibility is also distinct from experimental feasibility, which additionally requires that suitable conditions be identified and that the reaction proceed in acceptable yield in practice. Retrosynthesis proposals carry no conditions, and holding a model that reads them responsible for experimental outcomes would penalize it for information it is not given. The same reasoning applies to experimental records: a reported success provides evidence that suitable conditions exist, whereas a reported failure records an unsuccessful attempt without settling whether other reasonable conditions could work. Records of failed experiments therefore enter the evaluation set as candidates and are labeled under the same criterion as every other source.

Independence from the source of a reaction.

The criterion refers only to the listed reactants and products, not to how the reaction was produced. It therefore applies unchanged to proposals from retrosynthesis models, reactions edited by language models, experimental records and generated candidates, which is what allows performance to be compared across the sources of the evaluation set.

B.3 Decision procedure and recorded fields

For each proposal, the annotator records a label (feasible, infeasible or uncertain); one or more failure reasons if the label is infeasible (Section B.4); one or more notes if it is feasible (Section B.5); a difficulty rating; and a free-text note, which is required for uncertain and recommended otherwise. Uncertain is not a softened negative. It is reserved for proposals on which the annotator genuinely cannot decide, with the reason stated; an annotator who leans towards one label records that label.

Every proposal is taken through the ordered checks of Table B.3. Checks 1–3 take precedence: if one fails, its reason is recorded and later checks are not applied. Otherwise, checks 4–6 are assessed and all applicable reasons may be recorded. A proposal that passes all six is feasible. This precedence is part of the protocol. A defective proposal can often be described in more than one way—a missing amine partner, for instance, as an absent reactant or as a transformation without mechanistic basis—and without a fixed precedence, two annotators who agree that a proposal is infeasible may still record different reasons. Fixing the order makes the recorded reason reproducible. Two further rules apply. The reasons at check 3 are alternatives: missing_substantive_reactant applies when the intended transformation is recognizable and its only defect is an unlisted substantive partner, and reactants_cannot_give_product applies otherwise; if both are selected, only the latter is kept. Reasons from checks 4–6 may be recorded together when more than one applies.

B.4 Failure reasons

Table B.4 defines the seven reasons. They map onto the two conditions of Section 3: missing_substantive_reactant records a failure of completeness, and each of the other six records a failure of reactivity. Two distinctions guide the choice of reason. First, reactivity_conflict applies when the intended transformation is sound but a competing process prevents the products from being isolated, whereas reactants_cannot_give_product applies when the transformation has no valid basis to begin with. Second, competing outcomes do not by themselves make a proposal infeasible. If reasonable conditions could give the specified products in isolable form, even as a minor component, the proposal is feasible and carries a selectivity_concern note. It is infeasible only if no reasonable conditions could do so. The reason is reactivity_conflict when a competing reaction consumes the reactants or the products before the target can be isolated, and regio_stereo_violation when no available mechanism produces the specified isomer. Because catalysts and conditions may be assumed, a selectivity that a known catalyst or set of conditions can achieve counts as obtainable. A stereocenter or substitution pattern that the transformation does not touch, yet differs between reactants and products, is not a question of selectivity and is recorded at check 3 as reactants_cannot_give_product. Thus, an isolable minor regioisomer remains feasible even when another isomer predominates.

B.5 Notes on Feasible Proposals

Notes document the components or conditions assumed when assigning a feasible label. The four note categories are:

no_identified_caveat

Every species that must be physically added is already listed, and no material concern is identified. It does not claim that a complete procedure is given or that the experiment would succeed, and it excludes all other notes.

missing_auxiliary_reagent

A species permitted by Table B.1 is required but not listed, such as the base of an alkylation or the reductant of a reductive amination. The annotator names it and its role.

selectivity_concern

Competing chemo-, regio- or stereochemical outcomes are possible, but reasonable conditions could still give the products in isolable form.

harsh_conditions

Credible but demanding conditions, such as elevated temperature or pressure, are required. The conditions must remain compatible with the reactants and the products; hypothetical extreme conditions cannot rescue an otherwise unsupported transformation.

These notes document the assumptions accompanying a feasible label; the evaluation target is the binary feasibility label. Difficulty ratings record annotation effort and are not used in the reported evaluations.

B.6 Annotators and interface

Proposals were labeled by two annotators, a pharmacy faculty member and a postdoctoral researcher in chemistry, both with extensive knowledge of organic chemistry and wet-laboratory experience. Each proposal was presented in a web interface that renders the reactants and the products as structures from their SMILES, with the SMILES strings available on request. The annotators had no access to proposal sources or model predictions. The 4141 calibration reactions in the pool were settled during calibration. The 759759 reactions outside the calibration set were labeled independently under the final protocol, without access to each other’s labels.

B.7 Protocol calibration

Before the main annotation, both annotators labeled a calibration set of 5050 proposals under a draft of the guideline, 4141 of which belong to the annotation pool. The other nine calibration proposals are outside the pool and are not included in the released benchmark. Disagreements were discussed by cause, and the discussion was used to amend the guideline and align the annotators’ understanding. The labels of the calibration proposals were settled in the same discussion, so the 4141 that belong to the pool are part of the benchmark but are excluded from the agreement analysis of Section B.8. The amendments made the substantive–auxiliary test and its structural reading explicit (Section B.1), introduced the ordered decision procedure (Section B.3), and consolidated overlapping failure reasons into the seven of Table B.4. These amendments were in force for the whole of the main annotation.

B.8 Agreement and adjudication

Table B.5 gives the independent labels of the two annotators, before any adjudication, on the 759759 reactions of the pool that are not in the calibration set. Agreement was 77.9%, with Cohen’s κ=0.55\kappa=0.55 (95% CI [0.49, 0.61]). These statistics measure independent judgments before joint review.

Of the 168168 disagreements, 119119 were adjudicated by joint review against the written guideline. The remaining 4949 await adjudication and are excluded from the current benchmark and its reported evaluations. The benchmark therefore contains 591591 reactions with matching independent labels, 119119 with adjudicated labels, and the 4141 calibration reactions, totaling 751751 reactions from the 800800-reaction pool. Recorded reasons and notes are provided as supporting metadata where available.

B.9 Screening

Before annotation, every reaction from every source was screened with the general validity rules applied to the corpus (Section D.7). A reaction was discarded if its SMILES failed to parse or canonicalize, if it contained an unstable motif such as an O – O – O or B – O – O chain, if a product appeared unchanged among its reactants, or if a product contained more heavy atoms of some element than the reactants. The screen removes parsing failures and predefined structural patterns. The remaining reactions still require expert judgment. No additional structural screening was applied after annotation.

These filters define the structural scope of the benchmark; they do not implement the substantive–auxiliary distinction. Reactions that pass them are evaluated by the experts for completeness and reactivity under the stated criterion.

Appendix C Construction of the Benchmark

Section 4 presents the benchmark by source. This appendix describes how it was built, in the order of construction: curating positive reactions from ORDerly (Section C.1), generating negative candidates (Section C.2), collecting the reactions of each source (Section C.3), screening and annotation (Section C.4), and checking overlap with the training data (Section C.5).

C.1 Positive reactions

Positive reactions are taken from ORDerly (Wigh et al., 2024), a curated subset of the Open Reaction Database (Kearnes et al., 2021) with standardized atom mapping and yield annotations, starting from its retrosynthesis train and test splits. All SMILES are canonicalized with RDKit (RDKit, 2024). Reactions with a recorded yield of zero are removed from the positives and archived as candidates for the benchmark (Section C.3). We then discard exact duplicates and every reaction that violates a rule marked All or Positive in Section D.7: reactions that fail parsing, reactions in which a product component appears verbatim among the reactants, reactions containing an O – O – O or B – O – O chain, reactions in which a product contains more atoms of some heavy element than the reactants, and reactions with three or more highly similar reactant components. The curated corpus contains 801,276801,276 training and 76,63076,630 test positives.

C.2 Negative candidates

The five generation methods of Section 4.1 are applied to every positive reaction in both splits (Appendix D). Each candidate inherits the split of the positive reaction from which it was derived and passes the quality-control pipeline of Section D.7. Candidates derived from test-split reactions supply the generated source of the benchmark; the full output forms the generated corpus analyzed in Section 7 and .

C.3 Collecting the four sources

Table C.1 breaks the benchmark down by the model, language model or generation method that produced each reaction.

Retrosynthesis proposals.

For targets from the test split, we collected reactant proposals from eight single-step retrosynthesis models: LocalRetro (Chen & Jung, 2021), G2Retro (Chen et al., 2023), UAlign (Zeng et al., 2024), EditRetro (Han et al., 2024), Chemformer (Irwin et al., 2022), LlaSMol (Yu et al., 2024), and LARC (Baker et al., 2026) with two backbone language models, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Anthropic, 2024) and Mistral NeMo (Mistral AI, 2024). Proposals were pooled across models and deduplicated by canonical SMILES. They were retained whether or not they reproduce the recorded reactants, since both kinds belong to the distribution a model faces in deployment.

Zero-yield records.

From ORDerly we retrieve the reactions with a recorded yield of exactly zero that were removed during positive curation, apply the same canonicalization and validity rules, and remove any reaction whose canonical reactant–product pair also occurs among the positives. A zero-yield record shows only that the conditions tried did not give the product (Section B.2); these reactions are labeled under the same criterion as every other source.

LLM perturbations.

Recorded reactions from the test split were given to GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026a) and Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026a), which were instructed to modify the reactants or the product so that the reaction becomes infeasible while remaining superficially coherent. The instruction states the models’ intent only; whether a modified reaction is infeasible is decided by the annotators.

Generated reactions.

Generated candidates were sampled in equal numbers from the test-split output of each of the five generation methods (Appendix D). All 289289 are outputs of these methods, including those the annotators judged feasible.

C.4 Screening and annotation

Before annotation, every reaction from every source passed the screen described in Section B.9. The screened pool of 800800 reactions was then labeled under the protocol of Appendix B. The calibration, independent annotation and adjudication procedure yields the 751751 benchmark reactions (Section B.8).

C.5 Splits and overlap

The corpus follows the ORDerly retrosynthesis train/test split, and all benchmark reactions except the zero-yield records derive from the test split. No benchmark reactant–product pair occurs in the data used to train our models. Product overlap remains possible even when the complete reaction differs. 115115 benchmark reactions have a main product that is also the product of a training reaction, 9797 of them retrosynthesis proposals. BARTSmiles log-likelihood scores 76.676.6 AUROC on those 9797 proposals against 80.880.8 on the other 185185; this comparison is descriptive because the two subsets may differ in difficulty.

Appendix D Negative Candidate Generation

The generated reactions in the benchmark and the training corpus are produced by five generation methods. Each produces candidates intended to be infeasible, and whether a candidate is in fact infeasible is established only by expert annotation (Section 4.2). This appendix summarizes the procedures, their main settings, and the quality-control pipeline.

D.1 Design

Each method perturbs a positive reaction (𝐑∗,𝐏∗)(\mathbf{R}^{*},\mathbf{P}^{*}) along one of two axes. Reactant perturbations (RA, RR, NC) replace 𝐑∗\mathbf{R}^{*} with 𝐑~\tilde{\mathbf{R}} while holding the products fixed, whereas outcome perturbations (FT, ET) replace 𝐏∗\mathbf{P}^{*} with 𝐏~\tilde{\mathbf{P}} while holding the reactants fixed. All five methods are applied to every positive reaction in both splits, and each candidate retains a pointer to its parent positive, which supports pairwise training and method-level analysis.

D.2 Random Addition (RA)

RA modifies one or more reactants at the reaction center. Each reactant is reduced to its synthon by removing leaving groups, atoms drawn from a frequency-weighted distribution of common leaving-group atoms (e.g., C, O, N, halogens) are appended iteratively at the reaction center under valence constraints, for at most six addition steps per synthon, and the modified synthons are reassembled into reactants 𝐑~\tilde{\mathbf{R}}, giving the candidate (𝐑~,𝐏∗)(\tilde{\mathbf{R}},\mathbf{P}^{*}). Up to three candidates are generated per positive reaction. The modification is intended to make a reactant incompatible with the required bond-forming event. It does not guarantee a difficult candidate, and it can produce a reactant that still undergoes a related transformation.

D.3 Random Replacement (RR)

RR replaces the reactants with structurally similar reactants drawn from the positive training set. For each positive reaction, we retrieve the 200 most similar reactions by Tanimoto similarity on a joint reactant–product fingerprint and take as 𝐑~\tilde{\mathbf{R}} the reactants of the highest-ranked ones that are similar to, but different from, 𝐑∗\mathbf{R}^{*}. Up to nine candidates are formed per positive reaction, eight in this way and one from a reactant set drawn at random from the training set. The procedure does not verify that the replacement fails to give 𝐏∗\mathbf{P}^{*}, and it discards replacements whose Tanimoto similarity to the original reactant falls below 0.10.1 (Section D.7).

D.4 New Center (NC)

NC proposes an alternative disconnection of the product. The reaction-center model of G2Retro (Chen et al., 2023) predicts the top-10 candidate centers for 𝐏∗\mathbf{P}^{*}, and up to three centers that differ from the recorded one are retained, taken from the lowest-ranked end of the list. The resulting synthons are completed by RLSynC (Baker et al., 2024), which returns ten completions ranked by its value estimate, and the low-ranked completions are selected. A low rank indicates only that a completion is unlikely under RLSynC, not that the resulting proposal is infeasible.

D.5 Forward Template (FT)

FT applies forward reaction templates extracted from the positive training set to the recorded reactants, using RDChiral (Coley et al., 2019). We apply every template that occurs at least ten times in the training set together with up to ten randomly drawn rarer templates per reaction, and every product 𝐏~\tilde{\mathbf{P}} that differs from 𝐏∗\mathbf{P}^{*} under canonical SMILES comparison gives a candidate (𝐑∗,𝐏~)(\mathbf{R}^{*},\tilde{\mathbf{P}}). A product predicted by a template but not recorded for these reactants may nevertheless be feasible.

D.6 Elementary Template (ET)

ET enumerates elementary steps with 739 templates from the library of elementary templates of Joung et al. (2024). Starting from 𝐑∗\mathbf{R}^{*}, the templates are applied breadth-first for up to four steps, and every product reached in at least two steps that differs from 𝐏∗\mathbf{P}^{*} and is not recorded as a product of these reactants gives a candidate, with at most 50 candidates per reaction. As for FT, an unrecorded product is not necessarily infeasible.

D.7 Quality control

All candidates pass a unified pipeline of 16 rules in three tiers: general validity, negative–positive consistency, and removal of method-specific artifacts (Section D.7). In particular, no candidate may encode a product set that is a recorded outcome of the same reactants in the positive corpus.
